prompt_text:
The figure compares how different cells localize specific mRNAs to distinct intracellular regions, linking RNA position to where proteins are made. In bacteria such as *E. coli*, mRNAs appear distributed to recognizable subcellular sites including the nucleoid, cell poles, outer membrane, and more diffuse cytoplasmic regions, showing that even simple cells spatially organize translation.

In budding yeast, mRNAs are shown traveling to polarized destinations in the mother–bud system, including the bud tip, neck, mitochondria, rough or tubular ER, peroxisomes, and the nucleus/nucleolus. The drawing emphasizes transport along actin and localization near organelles, suggesting targeted local protein synthesis.

The animal examples extend this idea to larger polarized cells. In the *Drosophila* oocyte, different maternal mRNAs accumulate in opposite regions of the egg chamber, associated with anchored or sliding microtubules and transport from nurse cells, establishing embryonic axes. In the *C. elegans* embryo, selected mRNAs are enriched at the cortex or in germ granules, again indicating developmental patterning through RNA localization.

Finally, intestinal villus enterocytes illustrate a physiological switch: under famine versus re-feeding, localized mRNAs and ribosomes become enriched toward the apical, microvilli-rich region, consistent with nutrient-dependent reorganization of protein synthesis.

entities.name: oppositely localized maternal mRNAs in oocyte
